questions.q: State the SI unit of the decay constant λ and write the differential equation for radioactive decay. Explain the physical meaning of the negative sign.
questions.a: The SI unit of λ is s⁻¹ (per second). The differential equation is dN/dt = -λN. The negative sign indicates that the number of undecayed nuclei N decreases with time; dN/dt is negative because N is decreasing. A wrong answer (e.g., unit = s, or missing negative sign) reveals the student treats λ as a time rather than a rate, or thinks the number of nuclei increases.

questions.q: A sample has a half-life of 10 days. After 30 days, what fraction of the original nuclei remains? A student answers 1/30. Explain why this is wrong and give the correct fraction.
questions.a: The student incorrectly assumes linear decay (subtracting a fixed amount each half-life). Radioactive decay is exponential: after each half-life, the remaining fraction halves. After 30 days (3 half-lives), fraction remaining = (1/2)³ = 1/8. The wrong answer shows the student does not grasp the multiplicative nature of half-life.

questions.q: The decay constant of a radioactive isotope is λ = 0.0231 s⁻¹. Calculate its half-life and mean life. Show all steps with units.
questions.a:
Given λ = 0.0231 s⁻¹.  
Half-life T₁/₂ = ln2 / λ = 0.693 / 0.0231 s⁻¹ = 30.0 s.  
Mean life τ = 1 / λ = 1 / 0.0231 s⁻¹ = 43.3 s.  
Check: τ = T₁/₂ / ln2 = 30.0 / 0.693 = 43.3 s. Consistent.  
A wrong answer (e.g., T₁/₂ = λ/ln2) reveals confusion between λ and T₁/₂ formulas or unit inversion.

questions.q: Two radioactive samples A and B have the same initial number of nuclei. Sample A has a half-life of 2 hours; sample B has a half-life of 6 hours. Compare their activities at t = 0 and at t = 6 hours. Which sample has higher activity at t = 6 h? Justify.
questions.a:
At t=0: R_A = λ_A N₀, R_B = λ_B N₀. Since λ = ln2/T₁/₂, λ_A = ln2/2, λ_B = ln2/6 ⇒ λ_A = 3λ_B. So R_A(0) = 3 R_B(0).  
At t=6 h: N_A = N₀ (1/2)^{6/2} = N₀/8. N_B = N₀ (1/2)^{6/6} = N₀/2.  
R_A(6) = λ_A N_A = (ln2/2)(N₀/8) = (ln2 N₀)/16.  
R_B(6) = λ_B N_B = (ln2/6)(N₀/2) = (ln2 N₀)/12.  
Since 1/12 > 1/16, R_B(6) > R_A(6). Sample B has higher activity at 6 h despite lower initial activity.  
A wrong answer (e.g., A always higher) shows the student ignores that activity depends on both λ and remaining N.

questions.q: A student solves a decay problem using N = N₀ e^{-λt} and gets N = 120 nuclei at t = 10 s for N₀ = 1000, λ = 0.1 s⁻¹. Another student uses the half-life method: T₁/₂ = ln2/0.1 = 6.93 s, then N = 1000 × (1/2)^{10/6.93} and gets N ≈ 125. The first student claims the second is wrong because answers differ. Evaluate this claim.
questions.a: The claim is incorrect. The difference (120 vs 125) is due to rounding in intermediate steps. The exact value from exponential: N = 1000 e^{-1} = 1000/e ≈ 367.9 (wait, λt = 0.1×10 = 1, so N = 1000/e ≈ 368). The half-life method: T₁/₂ = 6.93 s, t/T₁/₂ = 10/6.93 ≈ 1.443, (1/2)^{1.443} = e^{-1.443 ln2} = e^{-1} ≈ 0.3679. Both give 368. The student's numbers (120, 125) are wrong for the given λ and t; they likely used λ=0.2 or t=20. The real issue: both methods are mathematically equivalent; any discrepancy is computational, not conceptual. The first student's claim reveals a misunderstanding that the two methods are different physical laws.

questions.q: Design a thought experiment to measure the half-life of a short-lived radioactive isotope (half-life ~ 1 minute) using a Geiger-Müller counter. List the key measurements, the graph you would plot, and how you would extract T₁/₂ from the graph.
questions.a: Measure count rate R (corrected for background) at regular time intervals (e.g., every 10 s) for ~5 minutes. Plot ln(R) vs t. The graph should be a straight line with slope = -λ. Half-life T₁/₂ = ln2 / |slope|. Alternatively, plot R vs t on semi-log paper; the time for R to drop to half its initial value directly gives T₁/₂. A poor answer (e.g., "measure time until counter reads zero") shows the student thinks decay completes in finite time or doesn't know how to handle background radiation.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: The law of radioactive decay states that the rate of ______ of a radioactive sample at any instant is directly proportional to the number of undecayed nuclei present at that instant.
Fill in the blank: Observe a glowing radium-dial watch in a dark room: its brightness ______ gradually but never reaches zero in a finite time.
Fill in the blank: Half-life (T₁/₂) is the time required for half the radioactive nuclei to decay: T₁/₂ = ln______/λ.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: Student can derive the exponential decay law from the differential equation dN/dt = -λN, calculate half-life and mean life from a given decay constant or activity-time data, and solve problems involving fraction remaining, time elapsed, and activity after multiple half-lives using both the exponential formula and the half-life method (N.
